text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno on Wednesday dismissed a clash between President Bill Clinton and the FBI as "a misunderstanding" and no cause for an independent investigation of campaign fund-raising issues.
"I think there was a misunderstanding," Reno said at a Senate Appropriations subcommittee hearing. "It does not in any way trigger the independent counsel statute."

She referred to a law requiring appointment of a special counsel, unconnected to the administration or the Congress, to investigate the conduct of high public officials when credible allegations of wrongdoing are lodged against them.

Reno has stoutly resisted pressure to seek appointment of such a counsel to probe the campaign fund-raising controversy embroiling Clinton and his Democratic Party. The pressure comes especially from Republicans who say a Justice Department probe and planned congressional hearings are not enough.

The FBI-White House clash began on Monday when Clinton backed up statements from aides that Federal Bureau of Investigation agents had briefed two members of his National Security Council staff last June on possible Chinese efforts to funnel campaign money to candidates in the 1996 congressional elections.

Campaign contributions from foreign governments are illegal, but Clinton said he had learned of the allegation only recently because the FBI briefers told their White House contacts not to pass it to higher-ups.

"Yes I believe I should have known," Clinton told reporters then. "No I didn't know. If I had known, I would have asked the NSC and the chief of staff to look at the evidence and make whatever recommendations were appropriate."

The FBI then took the highly unusual step of publicly contradicting a U.S. president, issuing a statement denying it had put any such restrictions on the Clinton aides. The White House took immediate issue with that statement.

Reno was drawn into her first public comment on the clash by questions at the Senate hearing. She said she assumed the White House staffers had been told the information about China -- which has angrily denied the charges of political meddling -- was sensitive, but that there was a misunderstanding over who else could be told about it.

Subcommittee Chairman Judd Gregg, a New Hampshire Republican, said he was concerned the dispute might jeopardise the Justice Department's own investigation of campaign fundraising. About 30 FBI agents are involved in the probe.
"Does it not put the Department of Justice in an untenable position to have its investigative arm in a public disagreement with the White House?" Gregg asked Reno.
"This doesn't concern the campaign finance investigation," she replied.

She repeated her familiar explanation for rebuffing calls to seek an independent counsel, saying, "I have not received from the (Justice Department) Public Integrity section information that they have specific and credible evidence of a violation of law."

She said she has told Justice Department investigators to pursue every lead and repeated her vow that she would ask a federal court to name an independent counsel if she received the requisite "credible evidence" of illegal activity.
The Senate's majority Republicans are threatening to pass a resolution formally requesting appointment of an independent counsel.
